subject: inflation
title: Why Things Cost More
summary: Inflation is when prices rise across many things, so each dollar buys a little less.

keys.answer: A general rise in prices over time, so each dollar buys less.

options.text: Many prices rising over time, so a dollar buys less
One store raising the price of one toy
Getting more money for free every year

keys.answer: They track a basket of everyday goods and services with a price index.

options.text: By tracking a basket of many everyday items
By asking one shop for one price
By counting how many coins are in a wallet

keys.prompt: What does mild inflation mean for your money?
keys.answer: Prices creep up a little, so cash left still slowly buys a bit less.

options.text: Cash left alone slowly buys a bit less
Every price falls overnight
Money stops working at stores

cards.title: Same candy, bigger price?
cards.text: Say last year a candy bar cost $1 at the corner store. This year the same bar is $1.20. Is that one change already "inflation"—or is something bigger going on?

cards.question: If just one candy bar costs more, is that enough to call it inflation?

options.text: Yes — any higher price is inflation
No — inflation is many prices rising together
Only if the candy is chocolate

cards.reveal: One product going up is not enough. The Fed says inflation is a general rise in the overall price level across goods and services.

cards.title: Prices rising together
cards.text: Inflation means prices of many goods and services rise over time. When that happens, each dollar buys a little less than before.
cards.example: Say… a lemonade cup, a soccer ball, and a movie snack all cost a bit more this year than last. That pattern is closer to inflation than one lonely price tag.

cards.title: A basket of stuff
cards.text: People measure inflation with a price index. Think of a shopping basket of everyday things. They check how the basket's total cost changes.
cards.example: In the United States, one famous basket measure is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI.

why.q: Why check a whole basket instead of one toy?
why.a: One toy can jump for many reasons. A basket shows if prices are rising in general.

examples_by_interest.soccer: Say… you track a ball, shin guards, and team snacks as a mini basket. If that whole set costs more next year, that is closer to inflation than one ball alone.
examples_by_interest.golf: Say… you track balls, tees, and a range bucket as a mini basket. If that whole set costs more next year, that is closer to inflation than one sleeve of balls.
examples_by_interest.business: Say… a lemonade stand tracks cups, lemons, and sugar as a basket. If that whole set costs more next year, that is closer to inflation than cups alone.

cards.title: Your dollar's stretch
cards.text: When prices rise, the same dollar buys fewer things. That is less purchasing power. Mild inflation means prices creep up slowly. Very high inflation means prices jump fast.
cards.example: Investor.gov says inflation reduces purchasing power. That is hard if you earn a fixed bit of interest.

cards.title: A little vs a lot
cards.text: The Federal Reserve aims for about 2% inflation over the longer run. Low, steady inflation helps people plan how to save, borrow, and spend.
cards.example: Say… prices rise a little and pay can keep up. That is different from prices jumping so fast a dollar feels smaller each month.

cards.question: What is one thing your family buys often? How would you notice if its price kept creeping up?
nudges: Think about snacks, sports gear, or a weekly treat.
Would one higher price convince you, or would you check a few things?

options.text: A general rise in prices over time
options.why: Yes. Many prices rising together, not just one item.

options.text: Finding a coupon at the store
options.why: Coupons lower what you pay. Inflation is about prices rising.

options.text: A bank giving you free toys
options.why: Inflation is about the price level, not free gifts.

questions.q: Why use a basket of goods to measure inflation?

options.text: It shows whether prices are rising in general
options.why: Right. A price index tracks a group of goods and services.

options.text: Stores only sell baskets
options.why: The basket is a measuring tool, not a shopping rule.

options.text: One candy bar tells the whole story
options.why: One price can move for many reasons.

questions.q: When inflation rises, what happens to a dollar left in a drawer?

options.text: It slowly buys less
options.why: Yes. That is weaker purchasing power.

options.text: It buys more every day
options.why: Rising prices mean each dollar stretches less.

options.text: It turns into more dollars by itself
options.why: Cash in a drawer does not grow. Inflation can shrink what it buys.

sources.title: What is inflation, and how does the Federal Reserve evaluate changes in the rate of inflation?
sources.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.supports: Inflation is an increase in prices of goods and services over time; it is a general rise in the overall price level, not one product; price indexes measure a group of goods and services; the Fed tracks CPI among other indexes; FOMC judges 2% longer-run inflation (PCE) most consistent with its mandate; low, stable inflation helps sound saving, borrowing, and investment decisions.

sources.title: Bonds - FAQs (Inflation risk)
sources.supports: "Inflation is a general upward movement in prices. Inflation reduces purchasing power, which is a risk for investors receiving a fixed rate of interest."; TIPS are adjusted based on changes in the Consumer Price Index.

sources.title: Consumer price index
sources.supports: A CPI is a weighted average price of a market basket of consumer goods and services; the annual percentage change in the CPI is used as a measure of inflation; in the U.S. the CPI is reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
